explanation.definitionFit: The thriller's full title puts this Greek word for 'twin' before Contingency.

clue.text: Baroness's investigative poet

parts.note: the Baroness is P. D. James, made a life peer; her police detective Adam publishes verse

explanation.walkthrough: P. D. James sat in the Lords as Baroness James; her Scotland Yard detective Adam is also a published poet.
explanation.definitionFit: P. D. James's commander Adam, a Scotland Yard detective, writes poetry between murder cases.

clue.text: French philosopher in some pretty candid eroticism

indicators.note: the answer is part of the following words, found inside them

explanation.surface: A French thinker is spotted somewhere in a frank piece of erotica.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in some' points to letters running across 'canDID EROTicism'; fittingly, Diderot wrote an erotic novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Denis Diderot, editor of the Encyclopédie, was a leading Enlightenment thinker from France.

clue.text: Mann cited disaster for him, poor beggar

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things in ruins, so the letters of the words before it are wrecked and rearranged

explanation.surface: Thomas Mann was quoted, a catastrophe for the wretched fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' scrambles MANN CITED into the answer; 'for him' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant lives by begging, typically a member of an alms-dependent religious order.

clue.text: Laws designed to limit Feuchtwanger's hero?

definitions.meaning: the British 'sus' laws let police stop and search people on mere suspicion, curbing their freedom
Lion Feuchtwanger's 1925 novel takes its title from its central figure, the court Jew Joseph Oppenheimer

explanation.walkthrough: The British 'sus laws' (from 'suspected person') allowed arrest on suspicion alone; Feuchtwanger's Jud Süss takes its title from its protagonist.
explanation.definitionFit: Süss is the court financier at the centre of Feuchtwanger's novel; the sus laws were Britain's suspicion-based stop powers.

clue.text: Swindle exceptionally dear, suggested by mischievous plotter against Hero

parts.note: to swindle is to con

indicators.note: something done exceptionally is out of the usual order, so the letters of dear are rearranged

explanation.surface: A con trick, unusually costly, is suggested by a scheming villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exceptionally' reorders the letters of 'dear'. Hero is the heroine of Much Ado About Nothing, slandered by Don John and his followers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing, this follower of Don John helps plot the slander of Hero.

clue.text: Miss Coleridge as novelist?

parts.note: Samuel Taylor Coleridge's unfinished poem has a heroine whose name a later Coleridge woman bore as a Victorian novelist

explanation.walkthrough: The heroine of S. T. Coleridge's poem shares her name with his great-niece, a Victorian writer of fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both the heroine of S. T. Coleridge's poem and that of the Victorian novelist Miss Coleridge.

clue.text: Scene of Herzog's highest endeavour

parts.note: Maurice Herzog led the 1950 French first ascent of Annapurna, the first eight-thousander climbed

explanation.walkthrough: Not Werner Herzog the film-maker: Maurice Herzog's book Annapurna recounts his 1950 summit of that Himalayan peak.
explanation.definitionFit: Annapurna, which Maurice Herzog climbed, stands in this Himalayan kingdom.

clue.text: He staged La Pucelle as a lark

definitions.text: He staged La Pucelle as a lark

parts.words: He staged La Pucelle as a lark
parts.note: La Pucelle is Joan of Arc; the dramatist's play about her is titled L'Alouette, French for the songbird

explanation.walkthrough: 'as a lark' seems to mean 'for fun', but it is the play's title: L'Alouette (The Lark), his drama of Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orléans.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Anouilh, the French dramatist, wrote L'Alouette, a play about Joan of Arc.

clue.text: "Sound the loud timbrel o'er 's dark sea" (Thomas Moore, Sacred Songs)

definitions.text: "Sound the loud timbrel o'er 's dark sea" (Thomas Moore, Sacred Songs)

parts.words: "Sound the loud timbrel o'er 's dark sea" (Thomas Moore, Sacred Songs)
parts.note: the gap before 's in Moore's hymn of the Exodus takes the land whose army drowned in the Red Sea

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Moore's line, which celebrates the Israelites' crossing of the Red Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Moore's song celebrates Pharaoh's host drowning, so the dark sea is that of the Nile kingdom.

clue.text: Dragon discouraging scrumpers

parts.note: scrumpers steal apples from orchards; the Greek serpent guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides

explanation.walkthrough: Scrumping is British slang for stealing apples from an orchard; the mythological dragon watched over the golden apples of the Hesperides.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this serpent-dragon guarded the Hesperides' golden apples until Heracles came.

clue.text: Bag party of writing

parts.note: a scrip is an old word for a small bag or satchel
the Tory party is Britain's Conservative party

explanation.surface: A satchel belonging to a group of writers.
explanation.walkthrough: SCRIP is an archaic word for a pilgrim's bag; TORY is a member of the British Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to written matter, as in a scriptorium.

clue.text: Singer at home to poet

parts.note: a songbird such as the skylark is a singer
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: A vocalist is at home to visiting poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is a bird here, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Larkin was the English writer of The Whitsun Weddings and High Windows.

clue.text: David changed its lamps

indicators.note: the letters of the words beside it are changed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone named David swapped out its light bulbs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changed' rearranges ITS LAMPS. King David is traditionally credited as author of the Psalms.
explanation.definitionFit: King David is traditionally the author of the Book of Psalms, so he is the sacred songwriter.

clue.text: Seeking college fellow at Wildfell Hall

parts.note: seeking is hunting
a don is a fellow of an Oxford or Cambridge college

explanation.surface: Looking for a university academic at a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Wildfell Hall is from Anne Brontë's The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, whose heroine flees her dissolute husband Arthur there.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur, the drunken husband in Anne Brontë's The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, bears this surname.

clue.text: A small-part actor is worth one more run

definitions.meaning: a film walk-on with no lines, part of a crowd scene
in cricket, a run not scored off the bat, such as a bye or wide, added to the total

explanation.surface: A bit-part player earns a further run.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the term covers byes, leg byes, wides and no-balls, each adding to the score.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean something additional: a supernumerary performer, and a bonus run in cricket.

clue.text: Posh utensil is obtained from sacred book

parts.note: U means upper-class, the classic label for posh usage
a pan is a kitchen utensil
had means obtained or got

explanation.surface: A smart kitchen tool comes from a holy text.
explanation.walkthrough: U for 'upper-class' comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U usage.
explanation.definitionFit: These are ancient Sanskrit philosophical texts of Hinduism.

clue.text: Usual CID I stirred up in historical novel

indicators.note: stirred up mixes the letters of the preceding words into a new order

explanation.surface: The usual detectives get worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of the British police.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Graves's novel is narrated by the Roman emperor and set in early imperial Rome.

clue.text: Philosophical interpreter of the cards in France

parts.note: in French 'of the' before a plural is des
French for cards is cartes

explanation.surface: A thinker reads fortunes from the cards in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interpreter of the cards' suggests a fortune-teller, but 'in France' says to put 'of the cards' into French.
explanation.definitionFit: René Descartes was the French thinker of 'cogito ergo sum'.

clue.text: Name of section (like Bleak, or An Ideal)

clue.text: It includes Hollywood hourglass for Redgauntlet

parts.note: Hollywood is in LA, Los Angeles
an hourglass is a timer

explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's Redgauntlet, the young hero Darsie goes by this surname, though he is by birth a Redgauntlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Darsie, raised under this surname in Scott's novel, is really the heir of the Redgauntlet family.

clue.text: Passage in Private Angelo, customarily overlooked

indicators.note: the answer sits in the words that follow, running across them

explanation.surface: A passage in Linklater's novel Private Angelo is usually skipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters across 'AngeLO CUStomarily'. Private Angelo is Eric Linklater's war novel; 'overlooked' is only surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A locus, as in locus classicus, is a passage of a text cited as authoritative.

clue.text: Bach's was well tuned

parts.note: Bach's keyboard collection is called Das wohltemperierte ..., so 'well tuned' is his title

explanation.walkthrough: Bach's preludes and fugues are The Well-Tempered followed by the German word for keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyboard instrument; Bach's 48 preludes and fugues are for the well-tempered one.

clue.text: Girl with the daddy of all Oedipus complexes

definitions.text: Girl with the daddy of all Oedipus complexes

parts.words: Girl with the daddy of all Oedipus complexes
parts.note: the daughter of Oedipus, whose father literally was Oedipus, the ultimate complex

explanation.walkthrough: 'the daddy of all' means 'the greatest', but here her daddy is literally Oedipus.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles' heroine is the daughter of Oedipus and his mother Jocasta.

clue.text: Bitter start of a cynical epigram recalling Baudelaire

explanation.walkthrough: 'start of' takes the opening letters of 'a cynical epigram recalling Baudelaire'.

a small catlike animal with a spotted coat related to the civet

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share the spelling: the French author Jean Genet, and the spotted civet relative.

clue.text: Josephus recounted its fall — also accounted for it

definitions.text: Josephus recounted its fall — also accounted for it

parts.words: Josephus recounted its fall — also accounted for it
parts.note: Josephus wrote The Jewish War on the Roman conquest of this province, and as its general he lost it

explanation.walkthrough: Josephus commanded Jewish forces in Galilee before defecting to Rome, then wrote the history of the province's fall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman province of Judaea, whose revolt and destruction Josephus chronicled in The Jewish War.
